instructions: Calm, warm science-documentary narrator. Unhurried, with a sense of wonder, clear articulation, a brief pause between sentences.

lines.text: This is a map of chaos in a language model that is fed its own output. At every step, a blend of the words it expects next, weighted by their probabilities, becomes its next input.
Each point is one setting of two knobs: how strongly the model's internal state is steered along a philosophy direction, and the sampling temperature.

Color marks chaos: a positive Lyapunov exponent, the standard test, meaning that two nearly identical states drift apart exponentially fast. Gray marks a repeating cycle; the darker the gray, the more strongly the loop is pulled into it.
Inside the chaos lie windows of order. We are heading into one where the loop repeats every six steps.
This window is a shrimp, a shape known from simple chaotic systems, with a body, legs and a head. The physicist Jason Gallas gave it its name.
At the lower end of the body lies a kite, where two different cycles both attract. Which one the loop settles on depends on where it starts.
Inside the kite is the hook: a sharp edge where the loop, always started from the same state, switches from one cycle to the other.
It is not a bifurcation: both cycles exist and attract on both sides. The edge is where the boundary between their basins of attraction crosses the starting state.
Below it lie striations: tongues in which neighboring settings lead to different cycles, alternating from cell to cell.
We have zoomed in about a hundred and eighty times in each direction, and every cell is a separate double-precision computation of the model.
